what: Thomas Stearns Eliot born in St Louis, Missouri, 26 September.
A year in Paris; friendship with Jean Verdenal, a French medical student. August 1911 in Munich, where ‘Prufrock’ is finished.
Harvard graduate study: Sanskrit and Pali with C. R. Lanman, the Upanishads, Buddhism, and F. H. Bradley’s philosophy.
Eliot arrives in England; meets Ezra Pound in September.

Jean Verdenal killed at the Dardanelles in May. Eliot marries Vivien Haigh-Wood in June. ‘The Death of Saint Narcissus’ is set in type for Poetry (Chicago) and withdrawn; its opening lines are reworked in lines 25–30 of the poem.
Joins Lloyds Bank’s Colonial and Foreign Department in the City of London in March. Prufrock and Other Observations published, dedicated to Verdenal.
‘Dans le Restaurant’ published in the Little Review; its last stanza, in French, is the source of the ten lines of ‘Death by Water’ that Pound let stand.
December: Eliot tells his mother his New Year’s resolution is ‘to write a long poem I have had on my mind for a long time’.
Parts I and II drafted, under the title ‘He Do the Police in Different Voices’.
Eliot’s mother, sister and brother visit London for ten weeks. His health breaks down.

Lloyds grants three months’ sick leave. Eliot goes to Margate in the middle of the month and stays until 12 November; on 4 November he tells his friend Sydney Schiff that he has written ‘some fifty lines’ of Part III, sitting in a shelter on the seafront.
To Paris, where Vivien stays; then alone to Lausanne for treatment by Dr Roger Vittoz. Parts IV and V written there.
Back through Paris. Pound goes over the typescript there and again by post, cutting it hard; Eliot accepts nearly all of it. Pound’s verdict, in a letter of 24 January: ‘Complimenti, you bitch.’
Eliot reads the poem aloud at the Woolfs’. Virginia Woolf: ‘He sang it & chanted it rhythmed it.’

Smyrna burns, 13–22 September, a month before the poem is published. The fire is not in the poem; Mr. Eugenides, ‘the Smyrna merchant’ of line 209, was already in the typescript Pound edited in January.
First publication, without notes, in the first number of The Criterion, Eliot’s own new magazine.
American publication in the November number of The Dial, again without notes. The Dial’s award for 1922, $2,000, is announced in the December number.

Boni & Liveright publish the first book edition in New York on 15 December, 1,000 copies, the first printing to carry the notes. Eliot said in 1956 that he had expanded them to make the book long enough.

Eliot inscribes Pound’s copy of the Boni & Liveright edition to him as il miglior fabbro, ‘the better craftsman’, Dante’s words for the poet Arnaut Daniel in Purgatorio XXVI; the phrase becomes the printed dedication in 1925.
The Hogarth Press edition, hand-set by Virginia and Leonard Woolf at Richmond, about 460 copies.
Poems 1909–1925 prints the dedication to Pound for the first time. Eliot leaves Lloyds for Faber & Gwyer.

Eliot records the poem at Columbia University, on aluminium discs, the earliest surviving reading. The discs were long dated 1935, and the PennSound archive still labels them so; the Poetry Archive dates them 1933, following the scholar Lacy Rumsey and the work of Richard Swigg (2012) and Jason Camlot (2019).
Eliot records the poem again; this later reading, dated 1946 by the Poetry Archive and issued on record, is the one most often heard.
In a lecture at Minneapolis, ‘The Frontiers of Criticism’, Eliot calls the notes ‘bogus scholarship’ and regrets having sent readers on ‘a wild goose chase after Tarot cards and the Holy Grail’.
Eliot dies in London, 4 January.

The New York Public Library announces that it holds the typescript, long thought lost, with Pound’s and Vivien Eliot’s comments written on it. Eliot had sent it in 1922 to the New York lawyer and collector John Quinn; after Quinn’s death in 1924 it passed to his sister and then to his niece, who sold it to the library in 1958 on condition of secrecy, and the purchase was not made public for ten years.
Valerie Eliot, his widow, edits a facsimile edition of the drafts, showing Pound’s cuts and comments.
Christopher Ricks and Jim McCue publish their annotated edition, The Poems of T. S. Eliot, in two volumes.
Centenary. The 1922 text is in the public domain in the United States; in the United Kingdom it remains in copyright until the end of 2035.
